2. **Suspect functions**: `gets`, `strcpy`, `strcat`, `sprintf`; `strncpy` (may leave no terminator); `strncat` (see below).
3. **Return values are checked**: `malloc` and `calloc` (NULL), `snprintf` (truncation), `read` and `recv` (fewer bytes than asked, or -1).
4. **Sizes are computed safely**: no unchecked `count * size` (use `calloc` or `__builtin_mul_overflow`), no `int` length passed to a `size_t` parameter without a negative check.
5. **Lengths from input are compared with real lengths** (the Heartbleed row).
6. **Pointer loops stop with `<`**, not `!=` (the Cloudbleed row).

blocks.prompt: A diff adds `char out[64]; strncat(out, user, sizeof out);` after `out` already holds a 20-character prefix. Is the size argument right?
blocks.reveal: No. `strncat`'s size argument is the maximum number of characters to *append*, not the total buffer size, and it always adds a terminator after them. With 20 characters already in `out`, appending up to 64 more plus the terminator can write 85 bytes into a 64-byte array. The correct bound is `sizeof out - strlen(out) - 1`, which is easy to get wrong, so most style guides prefer `snprintf` with an explicit offset and the truncation check from this lesson.

blocks.md: For every C copy, ask three things: where does the destination size come from (never sizeof of a parameter), where does the copy length come from (never unchecked input), and is the function's return value checked (snprintf truncation, malloc NULL, short reads). Defender view: run tests and fuzzers under AddressSanitizer in CI; in production, fortify and stack-protector aborts in crash logs (lesson 13) are real overflows, not flaky crashes.

blocks.question: `int n = snprintf(p, room, "%s", s);` returns 40 when `room` is 16. What happened?
options: snprintf wrote 40 bytes and overflowed
snprintf failed and wrote nothing
snprintf wrote 15 characters plus a terminator; 40 is the full length it wanted
The return value is undefined when truncating
blocks.explain: C's snprintf never writes more than room bytes (including the terminator) and returns the length the full output would have had. A return value of room or more is the standard signal of truncation.

blocks.question: Which line has the bug a reviewer should flag?
options: `void g(char d[32]) { memcpy(d, s, sizeof(d)); }`
`void f(char *d, size_t cap) { snprintf(d, cap, "%s", s); }`
`char b[32]; fgets(b, sizeof b, stdin);`
`p = calloc(count, sizeof *p); if (!p) return -1;`
blocks.explain: A parameter written as char d[32] is still a pointer, so sizeof(d) is 8, not 32: the copy length is wrong (and clang's -Wsizeof-array-argument warns). The other lines take the size from the real buffer or check the result.

lessons.title: Compiler warnings and hardening flags a C reviewer should demand

blocks.md:
Several bugs in this course were caught by the compiler once the right option was on: goto fail by `-Wmisleading-indentation`, the memory-safety course's format string bug (shown again below) by `-Wformat-security`, `sizeof` on a pointer by `-Wsizeof-pointer-memaccess`. So the build configuration is code to review too. A diff that turns warnings off is a security change, even if it touches no C file.

The reference list is the **Compiler Options Hardening Guide for C and C++** from the OpenSSF (Open Source Security Foundation, a Linux Foundation project). It splits options into two kinds:

- **Compile-time checks**: warnings that find likely defects before the program runs.
- **Run-time protection**: options that add checks or change the binary so that bugs which slip through are harder to exploit.

blocks.caption: Apple clang 21. Default flags report one problem; part of the OpenSSF set reports three and refuses to build the worst.

blocks.md: Three bugs, three security stories. The format string is the memory-safety course's CWE-134, now a build failure. The missing `break` gives role 1 the level of role 2, a privilege bug no memory tool would notice. The truncation from `unsigned int` to `unsigned short` is how a length of 70,000 becomes 4,464 (lesson 15 shows the same conversion in Rust). None of them stopped the default build.

blocks.title: OpenSSF options and what each one buys

scenes.caption: Compile-time warnings sit on the left: they find bugs before anything runs, at no run-time cost.
Werror turns chosen warnings into build failures, so a finding cannot be merged by accident.
Run-time protections sit on the right. They do not remove a bug; they stop the program, or make exploiting the bug much harder, when it fires.
A build-file diff that removes any box on this map is a security finding, whatever its commit message says.

blocks.md:
The run-time options in the guide's recommended set, in one line each (the course *Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI* explains the mechanisms):

- `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3`: replaces calls such as `memcpy` and `strcpy` with checked versions where the compiler can work out the destination size; level 3 also handles sizes known only as expressions. Needs `-O1` or higher.
- `-fstack-protector-strong`: puts a guard value (canary) before saved return data and aborts if it changed.
- `-fstack-clash-protection`: adds run-time checks that variable-size stack allocations are valid.
- `-fPIE -pie`: builds a position-independent executable, so address space layout randomisation can move it.
- `-Wl,-z,relro -Wl,-z,now` and `-Wl,-z,noexecstack`: linker options that make relocation tables read-only and the stack non-executable.
- For production code the guide adds `-ftrivial-auto-var-init=zero` (start uninitialized locals at zero) and `-fno-strict-overflow`, among others.

blocks.code:
--- a/CMakeLists.txt
+++ b/CMakeLists.txt
-set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -Wall -Wextra -Werror=format-security")
-add_compile_options(-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3 -fstack-protector-strong)
+set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -Wall -Wno-format-security")
+# fortify breaks the vendored parser build, disable for now
blocks.caption: A real-looking build diff. Commit message: 'fix CI build'. Review comment: this removes two protections; fix the parser warnings instead.

blocks.md:
How to review a diff like that: the parser that "breaks" under fortify is probably the code that most needs it, since fortify failures and format-security errors are usually real bugs. Ask for the specific warning, fix the code, and if a third-party file truly cannot be fixed, scope the exception to that one file. The OpenSSF guide also advises using blanket `-Werror` during development but not in source you distribute (it ties the build to specific compiler versions), while selective forms such as `-Werror=format-security` are fine everywhere.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: put the hardening flags in the shared build configuration and fail CI when they disappear; on Linux, tools that inspect compiled binaries, such as `checksec`, can confirm the protections are present in the *output*, not just in the build file. *Detect*: a fortify or stack-protector abort in production (messages such as "buffer overflow detected" or "stack smashing detected" in crash logs) means a real overflow fired. *Respond*: treat each such abort as a vulnerability report, not a flaky crash.

Warnings find bugs; hardening flags limit the damage of the bugs you missed. Review build files like code: a change that removes either, or adds -Wno-format-security or -fno-stack-protector, needs the same scrutiny as a change to authentication.

blocks.question: Which statement about `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` is correct?
options: It removes buffer overflow bugs from the source code
It is a warning flag with no run-time effect
It only works in debug builds with -O0
It adds compile-time and run-time checks to unsafe libc calls where the compiler can determine buffer sizes, and needs optimisation enabled
blocks.explain: The OpenSSF guide describes it as fortifying sources with compile-time and run-time checks for unsafe libc usage and buffer overflows, requiring -O1 or higher. It turns some overflows into aborts; the bug is still in the code.

blocks.question: A pull request titled 'silence noisy warnings' adds `-Wno-implicit-fallthrough` to the build. What should the reviewer ask for?
options: The list of switch statements that warned, each fixed with a break or marked as intentional fall-through
Nothing: fall-through warnings are style only
Replace it with -w to silence all warnings
Move the flag to the release build only
blocks.explain: Each warning is a switch where a missing break may give one case another's behaviour, as role_level showed. Intentional fall-through can be annotated so the warning stays on for new code. Silencing all warnings hides the next goto fail.

lessons.title: Rust: what safe Rust promises, and reviewing unsafe

blocks.md:
Recall from the memory-safety course: Rust's ownership rules and borrow checker reject use-after-free and dangling references at compile time, and indexing is bounds-checked at run time. Those guarantees hold for **safe Rust**. Some code cannot be written within those rules (talking to hardware, calling C, building fast data structures), so Rust has an escape hatch: the `unsafe` keyword.

The Rust book lists exactly five extra abilities, which it calls *unsafe superpowers*: dereference a raw pointer, call an unsafe function or method, access or modify a mutable static variable, implement an unsafe trait, and access fields of unions. It also stresses that `unsafe` does not turn off the borrow checker or Rust's other checks. What it does is shift responsibility: inside the block, the *programmer* promises that the rules hold.

The promise has a precise name. A function is **sound** if no caller using only safe code can cause undefined behaviour, whatever arguments it passes. An unsafe block is usually correct only because of checks in the safe code around it. So the review question is never "is this unsafe line right?" but "does the surrounding safe code guarantee everything this unsafe line assumes, for every possible input?"

`get_unchecked(i)` is an unsafe method that reads `slice[i]` without the bounds check. Its precondition is `i < len`. Here is a safe-looking function that forgets to establish it:

blocks.caption: byte_at is a public safe function, so any caller can trigger undefined behaviour. That makes it unsound, even though nobody wrote 'unsafe' at the call site.

blocks.md:
The debug-build message says it plainly: that check is optional and cannot be relied on. In a release build the read is undefined behaviour, exactly like C. In our test the optimiser turned it into a crash; with a different index or build it could just as well return a neighbouring byte.

Tools help a reviewer find and judge unsafe code:

- **Clippy**, Rust's official linter, has a lint `undocumented_unsafe_blocks` that flags unsafe blocks without a `// SAFETY:` comment explaining why the operations inside are sound. On the code above it flagged `byte_at` and accepted `byte_at_fixed`.
- **Miri**, a Rust interpreter, runs tests and detects undefined behaviour, including out-of-bounds accesses, use-after-free and data races, in unsafe code that fails to uphold its safety requirements.
- `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` at the top of a crate (a Rust package, the unit that Cargo, Rust's build tool and package manager, compiles) makes any unsafe block a compile error, for crates that should never need one.

blocks.code:
$ cargo clippy -- -W clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks
warning: unsafe block missing a safety comment
 --> src/lib.rs:3:5
  |
3 |     unsafe { *record.get_unchecked(i) } // UNSOUND: nothing checks i < len
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = help: consider adding a safety comment on the preceding line

blocks.md:
**Real case: CVE-2021-31162, a double free in Rust's standard library.** In March 2021 a GitHub user reported that `Vec::from_iter`, in a specialised fast path that reuses a vector's memory, could free an element twice. NVD's summary: in the standard library before Rust 1.52.0, a double free can occur in `Vec::from_iter` if freeing an element panics.

Two terms. **Drop** is Rust's cleanup step: when a value goes out of scope, its `drop` code runs and frees what it owns. A **panic** that happens during cleanup *unwinds*: Rust keeps dropping the remaining values on the way out. The report explained that the internal `drop_remaining()` dropped elements before updating its record of which elements remained, so when a later drop panicked, unwinding dropped the already-dropped elements again. The proof of concept began with `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`: the reporter's program contained no unsafe code at all.

blocks.title: CVE-2021-31162: how a panicking drop freed an element twice

scenes.caption: A vector holds two elements: A owns a heap box, B panics when dropped. The specialised from_iter path must drop the elements it no longer needs.
drop_remaining() drops A, freeing its box. Its record of remaining elements has not been updated yet: it still lists A as live.
Dropping B panics. Rust unwinds and, to avoid leaks, drops everything the record still lists as live.
The record says A is live, so A's box is freed a second time: a double free, reached from safe code. The fix updated the record before dropping.

blocks.md:
The lessons for reviewing unsafe Rust:

1. **Safe Rust is only as safe as the unsafe code beneath it**, including the standard library and every dependency. A crate with no unsafe of its own can still hit undefined behaviour through one that has some.
2. **Panic safety**: unsafe code must leave its data consistent at every point where something it calls might panic, because unwinding will run more code over that data. Update bookkeeping *before* the operation that can panic.
3. **Keep unsafe small and wrapped** in a safe API whose checks make it sound, and document the invariant in a `SAFETY` comment a reviewer can verify.

Google's Android team, writing in November 2025, described the same practice: unsafe code cannot be banned in an operating system, so they train developers in soundness, safety comments and encapsulating unsafe code in safe abstractions.

**Defender view.** Prevent with forbid(unsafe_code) and Miri in CI; detect by tracking advisories for std and your crates (RustSec, the Rust security advisory database); respond by upgrading and rebuilding.

Review unsafe Rust as C, with one question: can any input from safe code make this block break its preconditions? Require a SAFETY comment that names the check, keep the block tiny, think about panics in the middle, and run the tests under Miri.

blocks.question: A crate exposes `pub fn get(&self, i: usize) -> &T { unsafe { self.items.get_unchecked(i) } }`. What is the review finding?
options: None: the code compiles, so the borrow checker proved it safe
The function is unsound: safe callers can pass any i and cause an out-of-bounds read
It should use a raw pointer instead of get_unchecked
It needs #![forbid(unsafe_code)]
blocks.explain: unsafe does not make the compiler check the precondition i < len; the programmer must. A public safe function that lets callers violate it is unsound. Check i < self.items.len() first, or simply use self.items[i]. forbid(unsafe_code) would reject the code rather than fix it.

blocks.question: The CVE-2021-31162 proof of concept contained `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. What does that show?
options: The attribute does not work
Rust has no memory safety guarantees
Undefined behaviour can come from unsafe code in libraries you call, including std, not just your own
Panics are always memory errors
blocks.explain: forbid(unsafe_code) guaranteed the program itself had no unsafe blocks; the double free was inside the standard library's own unsafe implementation of Vec::from_iter. The guarantee covers your code, and relies on the soundness of everything beneath it.

lessons.title: Rust: FFI boundaries, release-mode overflow and panics

blocks.md:
Safe Rust removes memory bugs, not logic bugs. Three Rust-specific traps show up in reviews of otherwise safe code: integer arithmetic that behaves differently in debug and release builds, calls into C across the **FFI** (foreign function interface, the mechanism for calling functions written in another language), and panics that an attacker can trigger on purpose.

Start with arithmetic. The Rust book: in debug builds, integer overflow makes the program panic; in release builds (`--release`), Rust does not check and instead performs two's complement wrapping, so a `u8` value of 256 becomes 0. Cargo's default release profile sets `overflow-checks = false`. Separately, the `as` operator converts between integer types by silently truncating, in every build.

blocks.caption: Real output, rustc 1.90. The tests (debug) would catch the overflow; production (release) computes 464 and carries on.

blocks.md:
In safe Rust a wrong length usually cannot corrupt memory, because every index is still checked. But it can still be a security bug: a size limit that wraps lets an oversized message through, a quota that wraps resets to zero, an offset that wraps reads the wrong record. And if the wrapped value reaches `unsafe` code or C, it is a memory bug again.

What to ask for in review:

- `checked_add`, `checked_mul` and friends (returning `None` on overflow) wherever a value from input feeds arithmetic, or `saturating_*` where clamping is the intended behaviour.
- `u16::try_from(x)` instead of `x as u16`, so an out-of-range value becomes an error rather than a different number.
- Optionally `overflow-checks = true` in the release profile for code that parses untrusted input, accepting a small speed cost.

blocks.title: What to check where Rust calls C

scenes.caption: Safe Rust on the left, a C library on the right. The extern block in between is unsafe: the compiler cannot see what the C code does.
Strings: C expects a NUL-terminated char pointer. A Rust &str has a length and may contain a NUL byte, which C would treat as the end.
Lifetimes: a pointer passed to C must stay valid as long as C uses it. If C keeps it after the call returns, Rust may already have freed it.
Ownership: memory must be freed by the allocator that made it. CString::from_raw on a C-allocated string is undefined behaviour; calling it twice is a double free.
Lengths and errors: every size C returns or receives is checked, and C error codes become Rust errors. Each box needs a SAFETY comment.

blocks.caption: CString enforces the C string contract at the boundary. Passing name.as_ptr() from a &str instead would hand C bytes with no terminator.

blocks.md:
Why the interior NUL matters: if Rust checked that a file name ends in `.txt` and then passed `admin` NUL `.txt` to a C function, C would stop at the NUL and open `admin`. Validating in one language and using in another, with different rules about where a string ends, is a classic boundary bug. `CString::new` turns the mismatch into an error.

**Panics as denial of service.** `unwrap()` and `expect()` say "this cannot fail; if it does, panic". On input from outside, it can fail whenever the attacker likes. Indexing `v[i]` with an attacker's `i` panics the same way. Depending on the server framework, a panic kills a request, a worker thread or the whole process.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: checked arithmetic, try_from and no unwrap on input, enforced with Clippy lints such as `unwrap_used` and `cast_possible_truncation` in CI. *Detect*: the same panic message repeating in service logs from one route means someone is feeding it bad input. *Respond*: return an error for that input, and make sure one panic cannot stop the whole process.

Rust review checklist beyond unsafe: arithmetic on input uses checked_* or try_from, not + or as; every FFI call has a SAFETY comment covering NUL termination, pointer lifetime, ownership and lengths; and no unwrap, expect or unchecked index on anything an attacker controls.

blocks.question: A Rust parser computes `let end = offset + len;` with both values from a file, then uses `&buf[offset..end]`. In a release build, a huge `len` makes `end` wrap to a small number. What happens?
options: Memory corruption, as in C
Rust silently returns the whole buffer
The compiler rejects the code
The slice has end < offset, so slicing panics: a denial of service, not an out-of-bounds read
blocks.explain: Release builds wrap the addition, but slicing is still bounds-checked, and a range whose end is before its start panics. Safe Rust turns the C-style overflow into a crash. Use checked_add and return an error instead, so the bad file is rejected cleanly.

blocks.question: Which FFI call is correct for passing a Rust string to a C function that expects a NUL-terminated string?
options: `f(name.as_ptr() as *const c_char)` with `name: &str`
`let c = CString::new(name)?; unsafe { f(c.as_ptr()) }`
`unsafe { f(CString::new(name).unwrap().into_raw()) }` and never free it
`unsafe { f(name.to_string().as_ptr() as *const c_char) }`
blocks.explain: A &str or String has no terminating NUL, so C would read past its end. into_raw without a matching from_raw leaks memory, and unwrap panics on interior NULs. Binding the CString to a variable keeps it alive for the call and guarantees exactly one terminator.

lessons.title: Memory-safe roadmaps: CISA's guidance and Android's numbers

blocks.md:
Lessons 10 to 15 reviewed memory bugs one line at a time. Governments and large vendors now argue that line-by-line review cannot keep up, and that the bigger lever is *which language new code is written in*. A reviewer meets this argument in practice as policy: "new parsers must be in Rust", "this C module needs an exception". This lesson gives the sources behind those policies.

The memory-safety course introduced **The Case for Memory Safe Roadmaps** (December 2023), from CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency), the NSA, the FBI and partner agencies, which asks software makers to publish a *memory safe roadmap*: a dated plan for moving to memory-safe languages (MSLs). Two later documents made it sharper.

**Product Security Bad Practices** (CISA and FBI; version 1.0 October 2024, version 2.0 January 2025) lists practices the agencies consider exceptionally risky for software used in critical infrastructure. Its first entry: developing *new* product lines in a memory-unsafe language such as C or C++, where readily available memory-safe alternatives could be used, is dangerous. For *existing* products, it recommended publishing a memory safety roadmap by the end of 2025, prioritising network-facing code and code that handles sensitive functions, and it suggests a sequence: write new components in MSLs while adding hardware or compiler controls to the old ones. The same document also names SQL injection and command injection as bad practices.

**Memory Safe Languages: Reducing Vulnerabilities in Modern Software Development** (CISA and NSA, 24 June 2025) addresses the obstacles to adoption and recommends language-level protections, library support, robust tooling and developer training.

**The evidence: Android.** Google's Android team has published the share of Android's vulnerabilities that are memory safety bugs for several years. In September 2024, Jeff Vander Stoep (Android) and Alex Rebert (Google Security Foundations) reported that the share fell from 76 percent in 2019 to 24 percent in 2024, as development of *new* code shifted to memory-safe languages. Their explanation is that **vulnerabilities decay exponentially**: most live in recent code, and old code gets safer as bugs are found and fixed. Using measured vulnerability lifetimes, 5-year-old code has a 3.4x to 7.4x lower vulnerability density than new code. So you do not need to rewrite everything: stop adding new memory-unsafe code, and the total falls.

In November 2025 the team reported that memory safety vulnerabilities fell *below 20 percent* of Android's total for the first time.

blocks.title: Memory safety bugs as a share of Android vulnerabilities

scenes.caption: 2019: 76 percent, close to the roughly 70 percent seen at Microsoft and in Chromium. Android began moving new development to memory-safe languages around this time.
2022: 35 percent, the first year memory safety bugs were not a majority (Android 13 blog, December 2022).
2024: 24 percent, while most of Android's code was still C and C++. Most bugs live in new code, and new code was increasingly memory-safe. 2025 fell below 20 percent.

blocks.md:
Google's November 2025 post adds numbers a reviewer will hear quoted:

- **Density.** With roughly 5 million lines of Rust in the Android platform and one potential memory safety vulnerability found (and fixed before release), Google estimates 0.2 vulnerabilities per million lines of Rust, against close to 1,000 per million lines in its historical C and C++: more than a 1000x reduction.
- **Review cost.** Rust changes needed about 20 percent fewer revisions and 25 percent less time in code review, with about a 4x lower rollback rate than C++ for medium and large changes.
- **Unsafe.** About 4 percent of the Rust is inside `unsafe` blocks, and the team's data suggests it is less buggy per line than C and C++, partly, it suggests, because unsafe blocks get extra scrutiny.

The near miss: **CVE-2025-48530**, a linear buffer overflow in CrabbyAVIF (a Rust image decoder), was caught before any public release. Google says Android's Scudo hardened allocator made it non-exploitable: guard pages around its secondary allocations turn the overflow into a crash.

blocks.title: Estimated memory safety vulnerabilities per million lines (Android)

scenes.caption: Historical C and C++ in Android: close to 1,000 memory safety vulnerabilities per million lines, Google's figure.
Android's Rust: 0.2 per million lines, an estimate from one near miss in about 5 million lines. The bar is too small to see at this scale, which is the point.

blocks.md: Read the numbers as Google states them: one vendor, its own code, its own counting, and an estimate built on a single near miss. Correlation is not proof, as the [2022 post](https://security.googleblog.com/2022/12/memory-safe-languages-in-android-13.html) itself cautions. The direction is consistent across Google, Microsoft and CISA's sources, but a 1000x figure is not a guarantee for your codebase.

What this means when you review code:

1. **New code**: a new parser, network protocol handler or file-format decoder proposed in C or C++ deserves a question: why not a memory-safe language? Many organisations now require an exception for it.
2. **Unsafe in MSLs**: the 4 percent is where review effort concentrates. Lesson 14's checks (SAFETY comments, soundness, Miri) apply to every unsafe block in a diff.
3. **Remaining C and C++**: lessons 10 to 13 still apply, plus the hardening flags and hardened allocators, which the CrabbyAVIF case showed still matter.
4. **Interop**: the boundary between old and new code (lesson 15's FFI) is a fresh attack surface that a migration creates.

Memory-safety policy is now a review topic: new memory-unsafe code needs a reason, unsafe blocks in Rust get the most scrutiny, and old C and C++ keeps its hardening. Android's data says the payoff comes from new code, because vulnerabilities concentrate in recent changes.

blocks.question: According to Android's 2024 analysis, why did the share of memory safety vulnerabilities fall while most of the code was still C and C++?
options: All old C and C++ code was rewritten in Rust
Memory safety bugs stopped being reported
Vulnerabilities concentrate in new code and decay with age, and new code was increasingly written in memory-safe languages
Compilers began rejecting all memory-unsafe code
blocks.explain: The post argues vulnerabilities have a half-life: old code becomes safer as its bugs are found, so most new bugs are in new code. Moving new development to MSLs cut the inflow, and the share fell without a full rewrite.

blocks.question: A team proposes a new TLS certificate parser in C for a network appliance. Based on CISA's Bad Practices guidance, what is the strongest review question?
options: Why is a new network-facing component being written in a memory-unsafe language when memory-safe alternatives exist, and what is the roadmap?
Is the code formatted with the house style?
Has the parser been benchmarked against OpenSSL?
Does the parser have a README?
blocks.explain: The guidance calls new product development in memory-unsafe languages dangerous where alternatives exist, and asks roadmaps to prioritise network-facing code. A parser of untrusted network input is exactly the case it describes.

lessons.title: White-box review of a small app, end to end

blocks.md:
Time to put the course together on a whole application rather than one diff: a **baseline review** in OWASP's terms. The app is a 37-line Flask notes service (Flask is a small Python web framework; `@app.get(...)` maps a URL to a function). Users authenticate with a token and can read notes, search their notes, download attachments and save display preferences.

OWASP's cheat sheet orders a baseline review roughly like this: architecture, then **entry point analysis** and input validation, authentication and authorization, **data flow tracing**, business logic, cryptography, error handling, configuration. For an app this small, that becomes four passes:

1. List every entry point (route) and what it reads from the request.
2. Check authentication and, separately, authorization on each one.
3. Trace each request value to its sinks (lessons 1 and 2).
4. Check the language-specific hazards (lessons 3 and 4 for Python).

blocks.title: Four passes over notes.py

scenes.caption: Pass 1, entry points: four routes. Sources: nid in the URL, q and name in the query string, and the raw POST body.
Pass 2a, authentication: before_request runs for every route and rejects unknown tokens with 401. Good, and it sets g.user.
Pass 2b, authorization: get_note fetches any note by id. Nothing compares the note's owner with g.user. Finding 1: IDOR.
Pass 3, data flow: q goes into an f-string that becomes SQL. Finding 2: SQL injection, which also defeats the owner filter.
name goes through os.path.join into open(). Finding 3: path traversal, the lesson 2 bug.
Pass 4, Python hazards: the POST body goes straight into pickle.loads. Finding 4: code execution for any logged-in user (CWE-502).
Also noted: no CSRF protection is needed here because auth is a header token, not a cookie; that is a reason to record, not assume.

blocks.code:
# probe.py: Flask's test client, logged in as ana (token t-ana)
GET  /notes/2                              bob salary            # bob's note
GET  /search?q=diary                       {'ids': [1]}
GET  /search?q=' OR 1=1 --                 {'ids': [1, 2]}       # every note
GET  /attachment?name=a.txt                attachment a
GET  /attachment?name=../notes-secret.txt  server secret         # outside FILES
POST /prefs (pickled {'theme': 'dark'})    {'theme': 'dark'}     # pickle accepted
GET  /notes/1 (no token)                   401
blocks.caption: Real responses from the test client. Each finding is confirmed against code we own, in a test, never against someone else's server.

blocks.md: How would a scanner have done? Bandit on the same file reported four issues: the pickle import (B403), a hard-coded temporary directory (B108), the f-string SQL (B608) and `pickle.loads` (B301). It caught two of the four real findings and added one that does not matter here. It missed the IDOR, because no function call is wrong (the bug is a missing condition), and it missed the path traversal, because it does not follow data. These are the CWE Top 25's number 4 (missing authorization; IDOR's own entry, CWE-639, is number 24) and number 6 (path traversal).

blocks.title: Who found what in notes.py

scenes.caption: Rows are the four real findings plus Bandit's extra report. Columns: manual review with the four passes, and Bandit 1.9.4. 1 means reported.
Bandit found the two bugs that are visible as a dangerous call (f-string SQL, pickle.loads).
It missed the two that need context: whose note is this, and where does this path end up. The B108 temp-directory note is noise for this app.

blocks.caption: Fixed handlers, verified with the same probes. 404 for another user's note avoids confirming that it exists.

blocks.md:
Why each fix works: ownership is part of the same query that fetches the row, so there is no way to read a note without owning it; the SQL text is constant and `q` travels as a bound parameter (the `%` wildcards are part of the value, not the query); the attachment path is checked after resolving; and JSON can only describe data. Then the reviewer's last step on a baseline review: **variant analysis**, searching the rest of the codebase for the same patterns (`execute(f"`, `pickle.loads`, `os.path.join(` with request data, queries by id without an owner column) so each finding fixes a class, not one line.

**Defender view.** For an app like this in production, the four findings each leave a trace: sequential ids returning 200 for one token (IDOR enumeration), SQL syntax errors or unusual LIKE patterns in logs (injection probing), `..` in query strings (traversal), and a web worker starting other processes (deserialization). Logging the user and object id on every read makes the first one visible at all.

A baseline review is the four questions applied systematically: list every entry point, check authentication and authorization on each, trace every input to every sink, then sweep the language's hazards. Tools find the dangerous calls; only the reviewer finds the missing checks.

blocks.question: Why did Bandit miss the IDOR in get_note?
options: Bandit does not support Flask
IDOR only exists in JavaScript applications
The query used a parameter, which Bandit treats as a vulnerability
The bug is a missing ownership condition, not a dangerous function call, so there is no pattern to match
blocks.explain: Pattern linters flag calls and constructs. get_note uses a safe parameterised query; what is wrong is what it does not check. Only someone who knows that notes have owners and that callers should see only their own can spot it.

blocks.question: After fixing /search, a teammate says the owner filter in the query means SQL injection could never have leaked other users' notes anyway. What does the probe show?
options: The injected OR 1=1 made the WHERE clause true for every row, and -- commented out the rest, so all notes matched
They are right: the owner filter always applies
The leak came from the attachment endpoint
SQLite ignores the owner column
blocks.explain: With q = ' OR 1=1 --, the query became owner = 'ana' AND body LIKE '%' OR 1=1, and the trailing %' was commented out. AND binds tighter than OR, so 1=1 matched every row: the probe returned ids 1 and 2. Injection rewrites the very filter meant to protect the data.

lessons.title: Writing the finding and the fix so it gets merged

blocks.md:
A finding nobody acts on protects nobody. The last skill of a reviewer is writing: a finding must let a busy developer, who did not watch you trace the code, understand the problem, believe it, fix it correctly and keep it fixed. In an interview's spot-the-bug round, the explanation is usually scored as much as the spotting.

OWASP's Secure Code Review Cheat Sheet gives a finding template. Its core fields: **Title** (vulnerability type in component), **Severity**, **CWE**, **Location** (file and line or function), **Description**, **Impact**, **Reproduction**, **Recommendation** (specific fix guidance with code), **References**, plus status, owner and due date for tracking.

blocks.code:
Title:          Deserialization of untrusted data in POST /prefs
Severity:       Critical
CWE:            CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data
Location:       notes.py:36, prefs()
Description:    prefs() passes the raw request body to pickle.loads(). pickle can
                call arbitrary functions while loading (Python docs: "The pickle
                module is not secure").
Impact:         Any logged-in user can run code as the web server process: read
                the database and secrets, and change any note.
Reproduction:   Test client, token t-ana: POST /prefs with pickle.dumps({...}) is
                accepted (200). A payload that calls a function instead of building
                a dict would run it. Demonstrated with print() in a local test only.
Recommendation: Parse JSON and accept only known keys and values:
                    p = request.get_json(force=True, silent=True)
                    if not isinstance(p, dict) or p.get("theme") not in ("light", "dark"):
                        abort(400)
                Add the regression test below. Search for other pickle.loads calls.
References:     https://docs.python.org/3/library/pickle.html, CWE-502
blocks.caption: The OWASP template filled in for finding 4 of lesson 17. Every line is checkable.

blocks.md:
How to fill the hard fields:

- **Severity** comes from two questions: how bad is the worst outcome (code execution, data of all users, one user's data, a crash), and who can reach it (anyone on the internet, any logged-in user, only admins, only someone already on the server). Code execution reachable by every user is critical; a crash reachable only by an admin is low. Many teams express this with CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System, a 0 to 10 scale, now in version 4.0; Log4Shell scored 10.0 under version 3.1), but the two questions are what the score encodes.
- **Reproduction** should be a test or a request against your own copy, never a live system you do not own, and never more than needed to prove the point. Show impact with a harmless action.
- **Recommendation** names the fix that removes the class (parameters, JSON, a resolved-path check), not a filter that blocks one string, and shows the code.

blocks.code:
# test_prefs.py: regression tests for finding SR-4
import json, pickle
from app_fixed import app

H = {"Authorization": "t-ana"}

def test_prefs_accepts_json():
    r = app.test_client().post("/prefs", data=json.dumps({"theme": "dark"}), headers=H)
    assert r.status_code == 200 and r.get_json() == {"theme": "dark"}

def test_prefs_rejects_pickle():
    r = app.test_client().post("/prefs", data=pickle.dumps({"theme": "dark"}), headers=H)
    assert r.status_code == 400

$ pytest -q test_prefs.py            # against the fixed app
2 passed in 0.08s
# the same tests against the original app:
FAILED test_prefs.py::test_prefs_accepts_json - assert (500 == 200)
FAILED test_prefs.py::test_prefs_rejects_pickle - assert 200 == 400
blocks.caption: A regression test fails on the vulnerable code and passes on the fix. It keeps the bug from coming back in a later refactor.

blocks.title: A finding from review comment to merged fix

scenes.caption: The reviewer leaves a comment on the exact line: the problem in one sentence, the impact, the fix and a test to add.
The author pushes a fix together with the regression test, so the test proves the fix.
CI runs the tests and linters. The new test passes; on the old code it would fail.
The reviewer checks the fix removes the class, not just the example, and runs a variant search for the same pattern elsewhere.
Variants get their own tickets. The original is approved and merged; the finding is closed with a link to the test.

blocks.md:
**Tone.** Write about the code, not the person: "this query concatenates `q`", not "you forgot to parameterise". Adam Langley's analysis of goto fail is a good model: after showing the bug, Langley wrote of believing it was just a mistake and feeling very bad for whoever might have slipped in an editor and created it, and then explained what tests and review could catch it. Developers fix bugs faster when the review assumes good faith and shows the way out.

A short pull-request comment version of the same finding:

*`pickle.loads` on the request body lets any logged-in user run code on the server (CWE-502). Please parse JSON and allow only `theme` in (light, dark); suggested code and a regression test are below. I'll check for other `pickle.loads` calls.*

Do not overstate. "Critical, full compromise" on a bug that needs admin access and a rare configuration teaches developers to ignore your severities. Do not understate either: "minor input handling issue" for code execution gets it scheduled next quarter. State exactly what you proved and what you believe but did not prove.

**Practice, legally.** Review only code you own, open-source code, or targets you are explicitly invited to test, and report through the project's disclosure process.

- [PortSwigger Web Security Academy](https://portswigger.net/web-security): free labs on SQL injection, path traversal, access control, deserialization, prototype pollution and more. After each lab, write the server code you think it runs, and the fix.
- [OWASP Juice Shop](https://owasp.org/www-project-juice-shop/): a deliberately insecure web shop you run locally. Its source code is public, so you can do a white-box review: find a bug by reading, confirm it in your local copy, write the finding.
- [pwn.college](https://pwn.college/): free, structured practice on C memory bugs, to train the eye for lessons 10 to 13.

A good weekly habit: read one published security fix commit in a language you use, and before reading the advisory, write the finding yourself.

A finding is complete when a developer can act on it alone: what is wrong (line and CWE), why it matters (impact and who can reach it), how you know (a safe reproduction), how to fix the class (code), and how to keep it fixed (a regression test that fails on the old code).

blocks.question: Which recommendation is best for a path traversal finding in a download endpoint?
options: Reject names containing ../
Resolve the final path and refuse it unless it is inside the download folder; better, look files up by id; add a test with ../ and an absolute path
Log a warning when .. appears
Add a WAF rule for ../
blocks.explain: Blocking one spelling misses absolute paths and encodings, and logging or a WAF rule only detects. Checking the resolved path (or not taking paths from users at all) removes the class, and the test keeps it removed.

blocks.question: You found SQL injection in an internal admin-only report page that runs with a read-only database account. How should severity be described?
options: Critical: SQL injection is always critical
Informational: admins can be trusted
Reachable only by admins and limited to reads by the account's permissions: lower than the same bug on a public page, but still a real finding to fix
Not a finding, because the account is read-only
blocks.explain: Severity combines impact and reachability. Admin-only access and a read-only account both reduce it, but a compromised admin session or a malicious insider could still read data they should not. Say exactly that, and recommend parameterisation anyway.
